```{r project-note}

# ── Project Context ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# This demonstration uses the UCI Default of Credit Card Clients dataset
# (Yeh & Lien, 2009) as a structural proxy for individual-level credit
# behaviour modelling.
#
# The data comes from Taiwan in 2005. We are not claiming it directly
# represents Australian consumers. We are using it to show that the
# Invisible Debt Trap Flag — inspired by ASIC REP 788 indicators — is
# technically feasible to build using machine learning on repayment data.
#
# Australian market context is provided separately through RBA C1 and C1.2
# official statistics, which are analysed in a later section.
#
# Citation:
# Yeh, I-C. and Lien, C.H. (2009). The comparisons of data mining techniques
# for the predictive accuracy of probability of default of credit card clients.
# Expert Systems with Applications, 36(2), 2473–2480.
# DOI: https://doi.org/10.24432/C55S3H
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Project context noted. Proceeding with analysis.\n")
```

```{r load-data}

# Reading the CSV file from the dataset subfolder.
# We are keeping stringsAsFactors as FALSE so R does not automatically
# convert text columns into factors — we will handle that ourselves later
# when we know exactly which columns need it.

uci_raw <- read.csv("dataset/UCI_Credit_Card.csv", 
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Quick confirmation that the file came in correctly
cat("Rows loaded:   ", nrow(uci_raw), "\n")
cat("Columns loaded:", ncol(uci_raw), "\n")
```
```{r first-look}

# The first thing we always do after loading a new dataset is just look at it.
# This tells us the column names, what types R has assigned to each column,
# and the first few values so we can spot anything obviously wrong.

print(glimpse(uci_raw))
```
```{r drop-id}

# The ID column is just a row number — it has no analytical value.
# If we leave it in, some models might accidentally use it as a feature,
# which would give us meaningless results. We remove it now.

uci <- uci_raw %>%
  select(-ID)

cat("ID column removed.\n")
cat("Working dataset now has", ncol(uci), "columns.\n")
```
```{r missing-values}

# Before doing anything else, we check if any data is missing.
# Missing values can silently break model training or skew results
# if we do not handle them deliberately.

missing_count <- sum(is.na(uci))

if (missing_count == 0) {
  cat("Good news — no missing values found anywhere in the dataset.\n")
  cat("We can proceed without any imputation or row removal.\n")
} else {
  cat("Missing values detected:", missing_count, "\n")
  cat("Columns affected:\n")
  print(colSums(is.na(uci))[colSums(is.na(uci)) > 0])
}
```
```{r data-cleaning}

# ── Fixing Known Data Quality Problems ───────────────────────────────────────
#
# UCI has a few documented inconsistencies that we need to fix before
# any analysis. These are well known in the literature and affect how
# we interpret the demographic columns.
#
# Problem 1 — EDUCATION column
# The codebook says valid values are: 1=graduate, 2=university,
# 3=high school, 4=others. But the dataset also contains 0, 5 and 6,
# which are not explained anywhere. We recode these to 4 (others)
# so they do not sit outside the valid range and confuse the model.
#
# Problem 2 — MARRIAGE column
# Valid values are 1=married, 2=single, 3=others.
# Some rows have 0, which again has no documentation.
# We recode 0 to 3 (others) for the same reason.
#
# Problem 3 — PAY columns (repayment status)
# Value -1 means the customer paid in full that month.
# Value -2 also appears and likely means no consumption or balance.
# Both mean the customer is NOT delayed, so we treat -2 the same as -1.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

uci_clean <- uci %>%
  mutate(
    EDUCATION = case_when(
      EDUCATION %in% c(0, 5, 6) ~ 4,
      TRUE ~ EDUCATION
    ),
    MARRIAGE = case_when(
      MARRIAGE == 0 ~ 3,
      TRUE ~ MARRIAGE
    ),
    PAY_0 = ifelse(PAY_0 == -2, -1, PAY_0),
    PAY_2 = ifelse(PAY_2 == -2, -1, PAY_2),
    PAY_3 = ifelse(PAY_3 == -2, -1, PAY_3),
    PAY_4 = ifelse(PAY_4 == -2, -1, PAY_4),
    PAY_5 = ifelse(PAY_5 == -2, -1, PAY_5),
    PAY_6 = ifelse(PAY_6 == -2, -1, PAY_6)
  )

# Confirm the cleaning worked as expected
cat("Cleaning complete.\n\n")
cat("EDUCATION values now:", sort(unique(uci_clean$EDUCATION)), "\n")
cat("MARRIAGE values now: ", sort(unique(uci_clean$MARRIAGE)), "\n")
cat("PAY_0 min value now: ", min(uci_clean$PAY_0), "\n")
```

```{r full-audit}

# ── Full Data Quality Audit ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# The basic cleaning fixed the known issues. But we should also check
# for duplicates, unexpected values in other columns, negative amounts
# where they should not exist, and extreme outliers that could distort
# our models. This is what a proper data audit looks like.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


# ── 1. Duplicate rows ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# If two rows are identical in every column, one is likely a data entry error.

dup_count <- sum(duplicated(uci_clean))
cat("Duplicate rows found:", dup_count, "\n\n")


# ── 2. SEX column ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Valid values are 1=male and 2=female only.
# Anything outside this range is an undocumented value.

cat("SEX unique values:", sort(unique(uci_clean$SEX)), "\n")
cat("SEX value counts:\n")
print(table(uci_clean$SEX))
cat("\n")


# ── 3. LIMIT_BAL — credit limit ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Credit limits should always be positive.
# A zero credit limit makes no sense — the customer would not have a card.

cat("LIMIT_BAL minimum value:", min(uci_clean$LIMIT_BAL), "\n")
cat("LIMIT_BAL maximum value:", max(uci_clean$LIMIT_BAL), "\n")
cat("Rows where LIMIT_BAL is zero or negative:",
    sum(uci_clean$LIMIT_BAL <= 0), "\n\n")


# ── 4. AGE — customer age ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Ages below 18 or above 100 are almost certainly data errors.

cat("AGE minimum value:", min(uci_clean$AGE), "\n")
cat("AGE maximum value:", max(uci_clean$AGE), "\n")
cat("Rows where AGE is below 18:", sum(uci_clean$AGE < 18), "\n")
cat("Rows where AGE is above 100:", sum(uci_clean$AGE > 100), "\n\n")


# ── 5. PAY_AMT columns — payment amounts ─────────────────────────────────────
# Payment amounts should never be negative.
# A negative payment amount has no logical meaning.

pay_amt_cols <- c("PAY_AMT1", "PAY_AMT2", "PAY_AMT3",
                  "PAY_AMT4", "PAY_AMT5", "PAY_AMT6")

cat("Negative values in PAY_AMT columns:\n")
for (col in pay_amt_cols) {
  neg_count <- sum(uci_clean[[col]] < 0)
  cat(" ", col, ":", neg_count, "negative values\n")
}
cat("\n")


# ── 6. BILL_AMT columns — bill amounts ───────────────────────────────────────
# Bill amounts CAN be negative in credit cards.
# A negative bill means the bank owes the customer money
# (e.g. a refund was processed and it exceeded the balance).
# This is valid — we just want to know how many there are.

bill_amt_cols <- c("BILL_AMT1", "BILL_AMT2", "BILL_AMT3",
                   "BILL_AMT4", "BILL_AMT5", "BILL_AMT6")

cat("Negative values in BILL_AMT columns (valid — credit balance):\n")
for (col in bill_amt_cols) {
  neg_count <- sum(uci_clean[[col]] < 0)
  cat(" ", col, ":", neg_count, "negative values\n")
}
cat("\n")


# ── 7. Target variable check ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The target should only contain 0 or 1. Nothing else.

cat("Target variable unique values:",
    sort(unique(uci_clean$default.payment.next.month)), "\n")
cat("Any unexpected target values (not 0 or 1):",
    sum(!uci_clean$default.payment.next.month %in% c(0, 1)), "\n\n")


# ── 8. LIMIT_BAL outliers ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Extremely high credit limits could be genuine (wealthy customers)
# or data errors. We flag anything above 800,000 NT$ for awareness.

high_limit <- sum(uci_clean$LIMIT_BAL > 800000)
cat("Rows with credit limit above 800,000 NT$:", high_limit, "\n")
cat("This is", round(high_limit / nrow(uci_clean) * 100, 1),
    "% of the dataset\n\n")


# ── 9. Bill amount vs credit limit check ─────────────────────────────────────
# Bill amounts should not realistically exceed the credit limit by a large
# margin. A bill far above the credit limit could indicate a data error.
# We check Month 1 as a representative sample.

over_limit <- sum(uci_clean$BILL_AMT1 > uci_clean$LIMIT_BAL * 1.1)
cat("Rows where Bill Amount Month 1 exceeds credit limit by 10%+:",
    over_limit, "\n")
cat("This is", round(over_limit / nrow(uci_clean) * 100, 1),
    "% of the dataset\n\n")


cat("─────────────────────────────────────────────────\n")
cat("Audit complete. Review findings above before proceeding.\n")
```

```{r remove-duplicates}

# ── Removing Duplicate Rows ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# We found 36 rows that are exact duplicates of other rows.
# These are almost certainly data entry errors — the same customer
# recorded twice. Keeping them would give those customers double weight
# in the model, which is not fair or accurate.
#
# We use distinct() to keep only unique rows.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

rows_before <- nrow(uci_clean)

uci_clean <- uci_clean %>%
  distinct()

rows_after <- nrow(uci_clean)

cat("Rows before removing duplicates:", rows_before, "\n")
cat("Rows after removing duplicates: ", rows_after, "\n")
cat("Duplicate rows removed:         ", rows_before - rows_after, "\n\n")


# ── Documenting Known Data Characteristics ────────────────────────────────────
#
# These findings from the audit are valid data characteristics,
# not errors. We document them here for transparency in the report.
#
# 1. Negative BILL_AMT values (~2% of rows per month):
#    These represent credit balances — situations where refunds or
#    overpayments resulted in the bank owing the customer money.
#    These are kept as-is because they reflect real customer behaviour.
#
# 2. 497 rows where bill exceeds credit limit (1.7% of data):
#    Interest charges and fees applied on top of an already-full
#    balance can push the total bill above the credit limit.
#    This is a normal credit card phenomenon and these rows are kept.
#
# 3. 1 row with credit limit of 1,000,000 NT$:
#    This is one customer with a very high limit. It is kept because
#    it represents a real (if unusual) customer in the dataset.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Data characteristics documented.\n")
cat("Final clean dataset ready:", nrow(uci_clean), "rows,",
    ncol(uci_clean), "columns.\n")
```

```{r fix-remaining-issues}

# ── Fix 1: Standardise Column Names ──────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Every column is uppercase with underscores except the target variable
# which uses dots and lowercase. We rename it to match the rest.
# Consistent naming prevents confusion when referencing columns in code.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

uci_clean <- uci_clean %>%
  rename(DEFAULT = default.payment.next.month)

cat("Target column renamed to DEFAULT\n")
cat("Column names now:\n")
print(names(uci_clean))
cat("\n")


# ── Fix 2: Convert Categorical Columns to Labelled Factors ───────────────────
#
# SEX, EDUCATION and MARRIAGE are categories, not numbers.
# If we leave them as integers, R will treat age=2 as twice as much as age=1
# which makes no mathematical sense for a category.
# We convert them to factors with meaningful labels so R handles them correctly
# in charts and model training.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

uci_clean <- uci_clean %>%
  mutate(
    SEX = factor(SEX,
                 levels = c(1, 2),
                 labels = c("Male", "Female")),

    EDUCATION = factor(EDUCATION,
                       levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
                       labels = c("Graduate", "University",
                                  "High School", "Others")),

    MARRIAGE = factor(MARRIAGE,
                      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                      labels = c("Married", "Single", "Others")),

    DEFAULT = factor(DEFAULT,
                     levels = c(0, 1),
                     labels = c("No Default", "Default"))
  )

cat("Categorical columns converted to factors.\n")
cat("SEX levels:      ", levels(uci_clean$SEX), "\n")
cat("EDUCATION levels:", levels(uci_clean$EDUCATION), "\n")
cat("MARRIAGE levels: ", levels(uci_clean$MARRIAGE), "\n")
cat("DEFAULT levels:  ", levels(uci_clean$DEFAULT), "\n\n")


# ── Fix 3: Check Financial Column Outliers ────────────────────────────────────
#
# We use the IQR method to detect extreme outliers in the bill and payment
# columns. An extreme outlier is a value that sits more than 3 times the
# interquartile range above the 75th percentile.
# We do not automatically remove these — we just count them and decide
# whether they are genuine or errors.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

financial_cols <- c("BILL_AMT1", "BILL_AMT2", "BILL_AMT3",
                    "PAY_AMT1",  "PAY_AMT2",  "PAY_AMT3")

cat("Extreme outlier check on financial columns (IQR method):\n")

for (col in financial_cols) {

  col_values <- uci_clean[[col]]
  Q1         <- quantile(col_values, 0.25)
  Q3         <- quantile(col_values, 0.75)
  IQR_val    <- Q3 - Q1
  upper_fence <- Q3 + 3 * IQR_val

  outlier_count <- sum(col_values > upper_fence)

  cat(" ", col, "— upper fence:", comma(round(upper_fence)),
      "| extreme outliers:", outlier_count,
      "(", round(outlier_count / nrow(uci_clean) * 100, 1), "%)\n")
}

cat("\n")
cat("Note: Extreme outliers in financial columns are kept.\n")
cat("They likely represent genuinely high-balance customers,\n")
cat("not data entry errors. Removing them would bias the model.\n\n")


# ── Final Dataset Summary ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("─────────────────────────────────────────────────\n")
cat("Final clean dataset summary:\n")
cat("Rows:    ", nrow(uci_clean), "\n")
cat("Columns: ", ncol(uci_clean), "\n")
cat("Factor columns: SEX, EDUCATION, MARRIAGE, DEFAULT\n")
cat("Numeric columns: all remaining\n")
cat("Missing values: ", sum(is.na(uci_clean)), "\n")
cat("─────────────────────────────────────────────────\n")
```

```{r pay-column-note}

# ── PAY Column Naming Note ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# You will notice the repayment status columns go:
# PAY_0, PAY_2, PAY_3, PAY_4, PAY_5, PAY_6
#
# PAY_1 does not exist in this dataset. This is a known quirk
# of the original UCI data — it was never included by the authors.
# It is not a loading error on our end. The six months of repayment
# history are still complete, just named this way.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

pay_cols <- names(uci_clean)[grepl("^PAY_", names(uci_clean))]
cat("PAY status columns present:", pay_cols, "\n")
cat("Note: PAY_1 is absent — this is a known original dataset issue.\n")
```

```{r feature-utilisation}

# ── Feature 1: Utilisation Rate ───────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# This tells us how much of the credit limit the customer is actually using
# on average across the six months we have data for.
#
# A customer using 80% or more of their limit consistently is a warning sign
# — it means they have very little breathing room left on their card.
#
# Formula: average bill amount across 6 months divided by credit limit.
#
# Two edge cases to handle:
# 1. Negative bill amounts (credit balance) — we treat these as zero usage.
#    The customer is not using their limit, the bank owes them money.
# 2. Values above 1.0 — bills can slightly exceed the limit due to interest
#    and fees. We cap at 1.0 so the rate stays between 0 and 1.
#
# This feature is inspired by ASIC REP 788's persistent debt indicator
# which flags accounts where average balance stays at 90%+ of credit limit.
# We use this as a proxy — not a direct replication — because our data
# does not include Australian interest-charged month records.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

uci_features <- uci_clean %>%
  mutate(
    # Replace negative bill amounts with 0 before calculating
    bill_m1 = pmax(BILL_AMT1, 0),
    bill_m2 = pmax(BILL_AMT2, 0),
    bill_m3 = pmax(BILL_AMT3, 0),
    bill_m4 = pmax(BILL_AMT4, 0),
    bill_m5 = pmax(BILL_AMT5, 0),
    bill_m6 = pmax(BILL_AMT6, 0),

    # Calculate average bill across 6 months then divide by credit limit
    avg_bill = (bill_m1 + bill_m2 + bill_m3 +
                bill_m4 + bill_m5 + bill_m6) / 6,

    # Divide by credit limit — cap at 1.0
    UTIL_RATE = pmin(avg_bill / LIMIT_BAL, 1.0)
  ) %>%
  # Remove the helper columns we created — keep things clean
  select(-bill_m1, -bill_m2, -bill_m3,
         -bill_m4, -bill_m5, -bill_m6, -avg_bill)


# Check the result looks sensible
cat("UTIL_RATE summary:\n")
print(summary(uci_features$UTIL_RATE))
cat("\nRows where utilisation is above 80%:",
    sum(uci_features$UTIL_RATE > 0.8),
    "(", round(mean(uci_features$UTIL_RATE > 0.8) * 100, 1), "%)\n")
```

```{r feature-repayment-ratio}

# ── Feature 2: Repayment Ratio ────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# This tells us how much of the bill the customer is actually paying back
# each month on average. A low ratio means they are barely touching the debt.
#
# For example, a ratio of 0.05 means the customer is paying back only 5%
# of their bill each month — the other 95% rolls over to next month.
# That is the revolving trap in action.
#
# Formula: average payment amount divided by average bill amount
# across the six months.
#
# Two edge cases to handle carefully:
#
# 1. When the bill amount is zero or negative (customer has a credit balance
#    or no balance that month), there is nothing to pay back.
#    We set the ratio to 1.0 for that month — fully covered.
#
# 2. When the payment exceeds the bill (customer overpaid), the ratio
#    would go above 1.0. We cap it at 1.0 — you cannot repay more than 100%.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

uci_features <- uci_features %>%
  mutate(

    # Calculate repayment ratio for each month individually
    # When bill is zero or negative, ratio is 1.0 (nothing owed)
    ratio_m1 = ifelse(BILL_AMT1 <= 0, 1.0,
                      pmin(PAY_AMT1 / BILL_AMT1, 1.0)),

    ratio_m2 = ifelse(BILL_AMT2 <= 0, 1.0,
                      pmin(PAY_AMT2 / BILL_AMT2, 1.0)),

    ratio_m3 = ifelse(BILL_AMT3 <= 0, 1.0,
                      pmin(PAY_AMT3 / BILL_AMT3, 1.0)),

    ratio_m4 = ifelse(BILL_AMT4 <= 0, 1.0,
                      pmin(PAY_AMT4 / BILL_AMT4, 1.0)),

    ratio_m5 = ifelse(BILL_AMT5 <= 0, 1.0,
                      pmin(PAY_AMT5 / BILL_AMT5, 1.0)),

    ratio_m6 = ifelse(BILL_AMT6 <= 0, 1.0,
                      pmin(PAY_AMT6 / BILL_AMT6, 1.0)),

    # Average the monthly ratios across all six months
    REPAY_RATIO = (ratio_m1 + ratio_m2 + ratio_m3 +
                   ratio_m4 + ratio_m5 + ratio_m6) / 6

  ) %>%
  # Remove the monthly helper columns
  select(-ratio_m1, -ratio_m2, -ratio_m3,
         -ratio_m4, -ratio_m5, -ratio_m6)


# Check the result looks sensible
cat("REPAY_RATIO summary:\n")
print(summary(uci_features$REPAY_RATIO))

cat("\nCustomers paying back less than 10% of their bill on average:",
    sum(uci_features$REPAY_RATIO < 0.10),
    "(", round(mean(uci_features$REPAY_RATIO < 0.10) * 100, 1), "%)\n")

cat("Customers paying back less than 20% of their bill on average:",
    sum(uci_features$REPAY_RATIO < 0.20),
    "(", round(mean(uci_features$REPAY_RATIO < 0.20) * 100, 1), "%)\n")
```

```{r feature-min-repayment}

# ── Feature 3: Minimum Repayment Frequency ────────────────────────────────────
#
# This counts how many months out of six the customer made only a
# very small payment — specifically 3% or less of their credit limit.
#
# Why 3% of the credit limit? This threshold is inspired by ASIC REP 788
# which flags repeated low repayments as a problem debt indicator when
# a customer pays 3% or less of their limit for 8 or more months.
# We use this as a proxy across our 6-month window.
#
# A customer who hits this threshold in 4 out of 6 months is showing
# a persistent pattern of making the bare minimum payment — which means
# their debt is barely moving.
#
# The result is a count from 0 to 6.
# 0 = the customer always paid more than the minimum
# 6 = the customer paid at or below the minimum every single month
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

uci_features <- uci_features %>%
  mutate(

    # 3% of credit limit is our minimum repayment threshold
    min_threshold = LIMIT_BAL * 0.03,

    # Check each month — did the customer pay at or below the threshold?
    low_pay_m1 = as.integer(PAY_AMT1 <= min_threshold),
    low_pay_m2 = as.integer(PAY_AMT2 <= min_threshold),
    low_pay_m3 = as.integer(PAY_AMT3 <= min_threshold),
    low_pay_m4 = as.integer(PAY_AMT4 <= min_threshold),
    low_pay_m5 = as.integer(PAY_AMT5 <= min_threshold),
    low_pay_m6 = as.integer(PAY_AMT6 <= min_threshold),

    # Count how many months the customer hit the low payment threshold
    MIN_PAY_FREQ = low_pay_m1 + low_pay_m2 + low_pay_m3 +
                   low_pay_m4 + low_pay_m5 + low_pay_m6

  ) %>%
  # Remove all helper columns
  select(-min_threshold,
         -low_pay_m1, -low_pay_m2, -low_pay_m3,
         -low_pay_m4, -low_pay_m5, -low_pay_m6)


# Check the distribution of results
cat("MIN_PAY_FREQ summary:\n")
print(summary(uci_features$MIN_PAY_FREQ))

cat("\nDistribution — how many months at minimum payment:\n")
print(table(uci_features$MIN_PAY_FREQ))

cat("\nCustomers with low payments in 4 or more months out of 6:",
    sum(uci_features$MIN_PAY_FREQ >= 4),
    "(", round(mean(uci_features$MIN_PAY_FREQ >= 4) * 100, 1), "%)\n")
```

```{r feature-balance-persistence}

# ── Feature 4: Balance Persistence Proxy ─────────────────────────────────────
#
# This counts how many months the customer's bill amount was sitting
# above 80% of their credit limit.
#
# When a balance stays consistently close to the credit limit month
# after month, it means the customer is not meaningfully reducing their
# debt — they are stuck near the ceiling.
#
# This is a proxy inspired by ASIC REP 788's persistent debt definition,
# which flags accounts where the average balance stays at 90% or more of
# the credit limit for 12 or more months. We use 80% as a slightly earlier
# warning threshold across our 6-month window.
#
# Important: we only apply this check when the bill amount is positive.
# A negative bill means the customer has a credit balance — they are
# definitely not in a high-balance situation that month.
#
# The result is a count from 0 to 6.
# 0 = balance was below 80% of limit every month
# 6 = balance was above 80% of limit every single month
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

uci_features <- uci_features %>%
  mutate(

    # 80% of credit limit is our persistence threshold
    persist_threshold = LIMIT_BAL * 0.80,

    # Check each month — was the bill above 80% of the credit limit?
    # We only flag positive bill amounts (negative = credit balance, not stress)
    persist_m1 = as.integer(BILL_AMT1 > 0 & BILL_AMT1 > persist_threshold),
    persist_m2 = as.integer(BILL_AMT2 > 0 & BILL_AMT2 > persist_threshold),
    persist_m3 = as.integer(BILL_AMT3 > 0 & BILL_AMT3 > persist_threshold),
    persist_m4 = as.integer(BILL_AMT4 > 0 & BILL_AMT4 > persist_threshold),
    persist_m5 = as.integer(BILL_AMT5 > 0 & BILL_AMT5 > persist_threshold),
    persist_m6 = as.integer(BILL_AMT6 > 0 & BILL_AMT6 > persist_threshold),

    # Count how many months the balance was persistently high
    BAL_PERSIST = persist_m1 + persist_m2 + persist_m3 +
                  persist_m4 + persist_m5 + persist_m6

  ) %>%
  # Remove all helper columns
  select(-persist_threshold,
         -persist_m1, -persist_m2, -persist_m3,
         -persist_m4, -persist_m5, -persist_m6)


# Check the distribution of results
cat("BAL_PERSIST summary:\n")
print(summary(uci_features$BAL_PERSIST))

cat("\nDistribution — how many months balance above 80% of limit:\n")
print(table(uci_features$BAL_PERSIST))

cat("\nCustomers with high balance in 4 or more months out of 6:",
    sum(uci_features$BAL_PERSIST >= 4),
    "(", round(mean(uci_features$BAL_PERSIST >= 4) * 100, 1), "%)\n")
```

```{r feature-payment-delay}

# ── Feature 5: Payment Delay Count ───────────────────────────────────────────
#
# This counts how many months the customer had a delayed payment —
# meaning they did not pay by the due date.
#
# In the UCI dataset, the PAY columns use this coding:
# -1 = paid in full that month
#  0 = minimum payment was made
#  1 = payment was one month late
#  2 = payment was two months late
#  (and so on up to 8)
#
# We count any month where the PAY value is greater than 0 as a delay.
# Even one month of delay is a warning sign. Multiple months of delay
# is a strong signal of debt stress.
#
# The result is a count from 0 to 6.
# 0 = no delays at all across six months — customer always paid on time
# 6 = the customer had a payment delay every single month
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

uci_features <- uci_features %>%
  mutate(

    # Check each month — was there any payment delay?
    delay_m1 = as.integer(PAY_0 > 0),
    delay_m2 = as.integer(PAY_2 > 0),
    delay_m3 = as.integer(PAY_3 > 0),
    delay_m4 = as.integer(PAY_4 > 0),
    delay_m5 = as.integer(PAY_5 > 0),
    delay_m6 = as.integer(PAY_6 > 0),

    # Count how many months had a payment delay
    PAY_DELAY_COUNT = delay_m1 + delay_m2 + delay_m3 +
                      delay_m4 + delay_m5 + delay_m6

  ) %>%
  # Remove all helper columns
  select(-delay_m1, -delay_m2, -delay_m3,
         -delay_m4, -delay_m5, -delay_m6)


# Check the distribution of results
cat("PAY_DELAY_COUNT summary:\n")
print(summary(uci_features$PAY_DELAY_COUNT))

cat("\nDistribution — how many months with payment delay:\n")
print(table(uci_features$PAY_DELAY_COUNT))

cat("\nCustomers with at least one payment delay:",
    sum(uci_features$PAY_DELAY_COUNT >= 1),
    "(", round(mean(uci_features$PAY_DELAY_COUNT >= 1) * 100, 1), "%)\n")

cat("Customers with 3 or more months of delay:",
    sum(uci_features$PAY_DELAY_COUNT >= 3),
    "(", round(mean(uci_features$PAY_DELAY_COUNT >= 3) * 100, 1), "%)\n")
```

```{r debt-trap-flag}

# ── Building the Invisible Debt Trap Flag ─────────────────────────────────────

# High Risk is assigned through direct conditions because payment delays
# and extreme balance combinations are clear unambiguous signals.
#
# For the remaining three categories we use a stress score built from
# four signals. Each signal that fires adds one point to the score.
#
# Two calibration decisions made from the actual data distribution:
#
# 1. Early Flag threshold set at score >= 2, not >= 3.
#    Requiring 3 out of 4 signals simultaneously outside High Risk
#    was too restrictive — almost no customers reached it.
#
# 2. Minimum payment signal widened to MIN_PAY_FREQ >= 5, not == 6.
#    Using exactly 6 was too narrow — it excluded customers who showed
#    minimum payment behaviour in 5 out of 6 months.
#
# These thresholds are ASIC-inspired proxies across a 6-month window,
# not a direct replication of ASIC REP 788's Australian conditions.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

uci_features <- uci_features %>%
  mutate(

    # ── High Risk — direct conditions ────────────────────────────────────────
    # Very high balance with almost no repayment
    # OR regular payment delays — both are clear unambiguous signals

    high_risk_flag = (UTIL_RATE > 0.80 & REPAY_RATIO < 0.10) |
                      PAY_DELAY_COUNT >= 3,


    # ── Stress score — four selective signals ────────────────────────────────
    # Each targets a distinct stress pattern in the data

    # Very high credit utilisation
    sig_util     = as.integer(UTIL_RATE > 0.75),

    # Very low repayment relative to bill amount
    sig_repay    = as.integer(REPAY_RATIO < 0.10),

    # Minimum payments in 5 or all 6 months
    sig_min_pay  = as.integer(MIN_PAY_FREQ >= 5),

    # Balance persistently near the limit for 4 or more months
    sig_persist  = as.integer(BAL_PERSIST >= 4),

    STRESS_SCORE = sig_util + sig_repay + sig_min_pay + sig_persist,


    # ── Final flag assignment ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # High Risk first — then score determines the rest
    # Early Flag at score >= 2 means two stress signals firing together

    DEBT_FLAG = case_when(
      high_risk_flag             ~ "High Risk",
      STRESS_SCORE >= 2          ~ "Early Flag",
      STRESS_SCORE == 1          ~ "Watch",
      STRESS_SCORE == 0          ~ "Stable"
    ),

    DEBT_FLAG = factor(DEBT_FLAG,
                       levels  = c("Stable", "Watch",
                                   "Early Flag", "High Risk"),
                       ordered = TRUE)

  ) %>%
  select(-high_risk_flag, -sig_util, -sig_repay,
         -sig_min_pay, -sig_persist)


# Check the final distribution
cat("=== INVISIBLE DEBT TRAP FLAG DISTRIBUTION ===\n\n")

flag_dist <- table(uci_features$DEBT_FLAG)
flag_pct  <- round(prop.table(flag_dist) * 100, 1)

for (flag in names(flag_dist)) {
  cat(sprintf("%-12s : %5d customers ( %4.1f%% )\n",
              flag, flag_dist[flag], flag_pct[flag]))
}

cat("\nTotal customers flagged:", nrow(uci_features), "\n")

cat("\nStress score distribution (non-High-Risk customers only):\n")
non_hr <- uci_features %>% filter(DEBT_FLAG != "High Risk")
print(table(non_hr$STRESS_SCORE))
```

```{r flag-validation}

# ── Validating the Flag Against Actual Default Outcomes ───────────────────────
#
# This is the most important check for the flag system.
# If our Invisible Debt Trap Flag is meaningful, we should see a clear
# pattern — customers in higher risk categories should default at
# significantly higher rates than those in lower categories.
#
# If Stable and High Risk customers default at similar rates,
# our flag is not adding any value. This chart proves it either way.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

flag_default <- uci_features %>%
  group_by(DEBT_FLAG) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Customers  = n(),
    Defaulted        = sum(DEFAULT == "Default"),
    Default_Rate_Pct = round(Defaulted / Total_Customers * 100, 1)
  )

# Print the table first
cat("=== DEFAULT RATE BY FLAG CATEGORY ===\n\n")
print(flag_default)

# Visualise the default rate by flag category
flag_colours <- c(
  "Stable"     = "#27AE60",
  "Watch"      = "#F39C12",
  "Early Flag" = "#E67E22",
  "High Risk"  = "#C0392B"
)

ggplot(flag_default,
       aes(x = DEBT_FLAG, y = Default_Rate_Pct, fill = DEBT_FLAG)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.55, colour = "white") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(Default_Rate_Pct, "%")),

    x        = "Risk Category",

  ) +
```

```{r flag-validation-note}

# ── Observation on Flag Ordering ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# The default rate progression shows an important finding:
# Watch (18.4%) is slightly higher than Early Flag (14.8%).
#
# This is not a data error. It reveals that the Watch category captures
# customers with a single but powerful stress signal — particularly
# very low repayment ratio — which is individually a strong default predictor.
#
# Early Flag captures customers with two signals firing together, but
# those combinations can be less predictive than one severe signal alone.
#
# This is a known limitation of equal-weight scoring and would be addressed
# in a production system by using model coefficients (logistic regression)
# to weight each signal by its actual predictive strength rather than
# treating all signals equally.
#
# The High Risk vs Stable comparison (42.3% vs 12.3%) confirms the flag
# system successfully separates the most at-risk customers from the safest.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Key validation finding:\n")
cat("High Risk default rate:  42.3%\n")
cat("Stable default rate:     12.3%\n")
cat("Difference:             ", 42.3 - 12.3, "percentage points\n")
cat("High Risk defaults at", round(42.3 / 12.3, 1),
    "times the rate of Stable customers\n\n")
cat("Note: Watch > Early Flag ordering addressed in report discussion.\n")
```

```{r model-prep}

# ── Preparing Data for Model Training ────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Before training any model we need to make three decisions:
#
# 1. Which columns to use as predictors
#    We use the original UCI features plus our five engineered features.
#    We exclude DEBT_FLAG because it is derived from the engineered
#    features — using it as a predictor would be circular reasoning.
#    We exclude STRESS_SCORE for the same reason.
#
# 2. How to split the data
#    We use a 70/30 train/test split. The model learns on 70% and we
#    evaluate how well it generalises on the held-out 30% it never saw.
#
# 3. How to handle class imbalance
#    The dataset has 78% No Default and 22% Default.
#    We tell the model to pay more attention to the minority class
#    by using class weights. This prevents the model from simply
#    predicting No Default for everyone and calling it 78% accurate.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Select only the columns we want for modelling
# Remove DEBT_FLAG — it is our business output, not a predictor
model_data <- uci_features %>%
  select(
    LIMIT_BAL, SEX, EDUCATION, MARRIAGE, AGE,
    PAY_0, PAY_2, PAY_3, PAY_4, PAY_5, PAY_6,
    BILL_AMT1, BILL_AMT2, BILL_AMT3,
    BILL_AMT4, BILL_AMT5, BILL_AMT6,
    PAY_AMT1, PAY_AMT2, PAY_AMT3,
    PAY_AMT4, PAY_AMT5, PAY_AMT6,
    UTIL_RATE, REPAY_RATIO, MIN_PAY_FREQ,
    BAL_PERSIST, PAY_DELAY_COUNT,
    DEFAULT
  )

cat("Model dataset dimensions:\n")
cat("Rows:", nrow(model_data), "\n")
cat("Columns:", ncol(model_data), "\n")
cat("Predictors:", ncol(model_data) - 1, "\n")
cat("Target: DEFAULT\n\n")


# Set a random seed so results are reproducible
# Anyone running this code will get the same split
set.seed(42)

# Create the 70/30 train/test split
# createDataPartition ensures the class balance is preserved in both sets
train_index <- createDataPartition(
  model_data$DEFAULT,
  p    = 0.70,
  list = FALSE
)

train_data <- model_data[ train_index, ]
test_data  <- model_data[-train_index, ]

cat("Training set size:", nrow(train_data), "rows\n")
cat("Test set size:    ", nrow(test_data),  "rows\n\n")

# Confirm class balance is preserved in both sets
cat("Class balance in training set:\n")
print(round(prop.table(table(train_data$DEFAULT)) * 100, 1))

cat("\nClass balance in test set:\n")
print(round(prop.table(table(test_data$DEFAULT)) * 100, 1))
```

```{r train-control}

# ── Setting Up Training Controls ─────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Before training any model we define how the training process works.
# This is the same control object used for all three models so the
# comparison between them is fair — same folds, same class weights.
#
# Two important settings:
#
# 1. Cross-validation with 5 folds
#    Instead of training on all 70% at once, we split the training set
#    into 5 parts. The model trains on 4 parts and validates on the 5th,
#    rotating through all five combinations. This gives a more reliable
#    estimate of performance than a single split.
#
# 2. Class weights to handle imbalance
#    We give the minority class (Default) roughly 3.5 times more weight
#    than the majority class (No Default). This reflects the 78/22 split
#    and stops the model from ignoring the Default class entirely.
#    The weight ratio is calculated from the actual class counts.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Calculate class weights from the training data
no_default_count <- sum(train_data$DEFAULT == "No Default")
default_count    <- sum(train_data$DEFAULT == "Default")

weight_ratio <- round(no_default_count / default_count, 2)

cat("No Default count in training set:", no_default_count, "\n")
cat("Default count in training set:   ", default_count, "\n")
cat("Weight ratio applied to Default: ", weight_ratio, "\n\n")

# Build the model weights vector
# Each row in the training data gets a weight based on its class
model_weights <- ifelse(
  train_data$DEFAULT == "Default",
  weight_ratio,
  1.0
)

cat("Weight for Default rows:    ", weight_ratio, "\n")
cat("Weight for No Default rows: ", 1.0, "\n\n")


# Set up the cross-validation control
# This is shared across all three models for a fair comparison
train_control <- trainControl(
  method          = "cv",
  number          = 5,
  classProbs      = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
  savePredictions = "final"
)

cat("Training control configured:\n")
cat("Method: 5-fold cross-validation\n")
cat("Class probabilities: enabled\n")
cat("Summary function: ROC / Sensitivity / Specificity\n")
```

```{r fix-factor-levels}

# The DEFAULT column has levels "No Default" and "Default"
# The space in "No Default" is not a valid R variable name
# caret's twoClassSummary requires valid R variable names
# We rename "No Default" to "No_Default" to fix this

train_data <- train_data %>%
  mutate(DEFAULT = recode_factor(DEFAULT,
                                  "No Default" = "No_Default",
                                  "Default"    = "Default"))

test_data <- test_data %>%
  mutate(DEFAULT = recode_factor(DEFAULT,
                                  "No Default" = "No_Default",
                                  "Default"    = "Default"))

# Rebuild model weights with the corrected level name
model_weights <- ifelse(
  train_data$DEFAULT == "Default",
  weight_ratio,
  1.0
)

cat("Factor levels fixed.\n")
cat("Training set levels:", levels(train_data$DEFAULT), "\n")
cat("Test set levels:    ", levels(test_data$DEFAULT), "\n")
```
```{r logistic-regression}

# ── Model 1: Logistic Regression ─────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Logistic regression is our baseline model — the simplest approach.
# It estimates the probability that a customer will default based on
# a weighted combination of the input features.
#
# We use it first because:
# - It is easy to interpret — each feature gets a coefficient that shows
#   how much it pushes the probability up or down
# - It trains fast — good for checking that everything is working
# - It is the academic baseline for credit risk models
# - It was covered in Week 7 of FIT5145
#
# We use the glm method (Generalised Linear Model) with binomial family
# which is the standard implementation of logistic regression in R.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Training Logistic Regression — please wait...\n\n")

set.seed(42)

model_lr <- train(
  DEFAULT ~ .,
  data     = train_data,
  method   = "glm",
  family   = "binomial",
  trControl = train_control,
  weights  = model_weights,
  metric   = "ROC"
)

cat("Logistic Regression training complete.\n\n")

# Make predictions on the test set
pred_lr       <- predict(model_lr, newdata = test_data)
pred_lr_prob  <- predict(model_lr, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")

# Build confusion matrix
cm_lr <- confusionMatrix(
  data      = pred_lr,
  reference = test_data$DEFAULT,
  positive  = "Default"
)

# Print results
cat("=== LOGISTIC REGRESSION RESULTS ===\n\n")
cat("Confusion Matrix:\n")
print(cm_lr$table)

cat("\nKey Metrics:\n")
cat("Accuracy: ", round(cm_lr$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("Precision:", round(cm_lr$byClass["Precision"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("Recall:   ", round(cm_lr$byClass["Recall"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("F1 Score: ", round(cm_lr$byClass["F1"] * 100, 1), "%\n")

# Calculate AUC
roc_lr  <- roc(
  response  = test_data$DEFAULT,
  predictor = pred_lr_prob[, "Default"],
  levels    = c("No_Default", "Default")
)

cat("AUC:      ", round(auc(roc_lr), 3), "\n")
```

```{r roc-curve}

# ── ROC Curve ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# The ROC curve is the standard academic visualisation for binary classifiers.
# It plots the True Positive Rate against the False Positive Rate at every
# possible decision threshold. The area under the curve (AUC) summaries
# the model's overall discriminate ability in one number.
#
# A perfect model would hug the top-left corner (AUC = 1.0).
# A random model would follow the diagonal line (AUC = 0.5).
# Our model at 0.766 sits meaningfully above random.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Extract ROC curve coordinates for plotting
roc_df <- data.frame(
  FPR       = 1 - roc_lr$specificities,
  TPR       = roc_lr$sensitivities
)

auc_value <- round(auc(roc_lr), 3)

ggplot(roc_df, aes(x = FPR, y = TPR)) +

  # The diagonal reference line — this is what a random model looks like
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.7) +

  # The actual ROC curve
  geom_line(colour = "#2471A3", linewidth = 1.2) +

  # Shade the area under the curve
  geom_area(fill = "#2471A3", alpha = 0.12) +

  # Annotate the AUC value directly on the chart
  annotate("text",
           x     = 0.65,
           y     = 0.25,
           label = paste0("AUC = ", auc_value),
           size  = 5,
           fontface = "bold",
           colour   = "#2471A3") +

  # Annotate the random baseline
  annotate("text",
           x     = 0.72,
           y     = 0.62,
           label = "Random classifier\n(AUC = 0.5)",
           size  = 3.5,
           colour = "grey50",
           angle  = 38) +

  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +

  labs(
    title    = "ROC Curve — Logistic Regression",
    subtitle = "Receiver Operating Characteristic | Default prediction on UCI credit card data",
    x        = "False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity)",
    y        = "True Positive Rate (Sensitivity / Recall)",
    caption  = "Source: Yeh & Lien (2009) | UCI ML Repository"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 10),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

```{r confusion-matrix-heatmap}

# ── Confusion Matrix Heatmap ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# A styled heatmap version of the confusion matrix.
# The four cells tell the full story of model performance:
#
# True Negative  (top-left):  correctly predicted No Default
# False Positive (top-right): predicted Default but was actually No Default
# False Negative (bot-left):  predicted No Default but was actually Default
# True Positive  (bot-right): correctly predicted Default
#
# For a debt stress system, False Negatives are the dangerous misses —
# these are genuinely at-risk customers the model failed to flag.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Build a clean data frame from the confusion matrix
cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm_lr$table) %>%
  rename(Predicted = Prediction, Actual = Reference) %>%
  mutate(
    Label = case_when(
      Predicted == "No_Default" & Actual == "No_Default" ~
        paste0("True Negative\n", comma(Freq)),
      Predicted == "Default"    & Actual == "No_Default" ~
        paste0("False Positive\n", comma(Freq)),
      Predicted == "No_Default" & Actual == "Default"    ~
        paste0("False Negative\n", comma(Freq)),
      Predicted == "Default"    & Actual == "Default"    ~
        paste0("True Positive\n", comma(Freq))
    ),
    Fill_Value = Freq
  )

ggplot(cm_df, aes(x = Actual, y = Predicted, fill = Fill_Value)) +

  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 2) +

  geom_text(aes(label = Label),
            size     = 4.5,
            fontface = "bold",
            colour   = "white") +

  scale_fill_gradient(
    low  = "#AED6F1",
    high = "#1A5276"
  ) +

  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("No_Default" = "No Default",
                                "Default"    = "Default")) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = c("No_Default" = "No Default",
                                "Default"    = "Default")) +

  labs(
    title    = "Confusion Matrix — Logistic Regression",
    subtitle = "Predictions vs actual outcomes on held-out test set (n = 8,989)",
    x        = "Actual Class",
    y        = "Predicted Class",
    caption  = "Darker = higher count"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 10),
    legend.position  = "none",
    panel.grid       = element_blank(),
    axis.text        = element_text(size = 11)
  )
```

```{r metrics-dashboard}

# ── Performance Metrics Dashboard ────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# A clean horizontal bar chart showing all four evaluation metrics
# side by side. This format is used in published ML papers because it
# lets you compare metrics at a glance without scanning a table.
#
# We include a reference line at 50% to show what random guessing
# would produce, and at 77.9% to show the naive baseline accuracy
# (always predicting No Default).
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

metrics_lr <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1 Score", "AUC"),
  Value  = c(
    round(cm_lr$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 1),
    round(cm_lr$byClass["Precision"] * 100, 1),
    round(cm_lr$byClass["Recall"] * 100, 1),
    round(cm_lr$byClass["F1"] * 100, 1),
    round(auc(roc_lr) * 100, 1)
  )
) %>%
  mutate(Metric = factor(Metric,
                          levels = c("AUC", "F1 Score", "Recall",
                                     "Precision", "Accuracy")))

ggplot(metrics_lr, aes(x = Value, y = Metric, fill = Metric)) +

  # Naive baseline — always predict majority class
  geom_vline(xintercept = 77.9,
             linetype   = "dashed",
             colour     = "grey60",
             linewidth  = 0.8) +

  # Random baseline
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50,
             linetype   = "dotted",
             colour     = "grey80",
             linewidth  = 0.8) +

  geom_bar(stat    = "identity",
           width   = 0.55,
           colour  = "white") +

  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(Value, "%")),
            hjust    = -0.2,
            size     = 4,
            fontface = "bold") +

  # Annotate the reference lines
  annotate("text", x = 79, y = 0.5,
           label  = "Naive\nbaseline\n77.9%",
           size   = 3, colour = "grey50", hjust = 0) +

  annotate("text", x = 51, y = 0.5,
           label  = "Random\n50%",
           size   = 3, colour = "grey70", hjust = 0) +

  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Accuracy"  = "#2471A3",
    "Precision" = "#1A9E6A",
    "Recall"    = "#E67E22",
    "F1 Score"  = "#8E44AD",
    "AUC"       = "#C0392B"
  )) +

  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +

  labs(
    title    = "Model Performance Dashboard — Logistic Regression",
    subtitle = "All metrics evaluated on held-out test set (n = 8,989)",
    x        = "Score (%)",
    y        = NULL,
    caption  = "Dashed line = naive baseline (always predict majority class)"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "none",
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),

    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y      = element_text(size = 12)
  )
```

```{r classification-tree}

# ── Model 2: Classification Tree ─────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# A classification tree splits customers into groups by asking a series
# of yes or no questions about their features. Each split tries to
# separate defaulters from non-defaulters as cleanly as possible.
#
# We use it because:
# - It produces a visual decision tree we can read and explain
# - It shows exactly which features matter and at what thresholds
# - It directly reflects the logic behind our Invisible Debt Trap Flag
# - It was covered in Week 7 of FIT5145
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Training Classification Tree — please wait...\n\n")

set.seed(42)

model_tree <- train(
  DEFAULT ~ .,
  data       = train_data,
  method     = "rpart",
  trControl  = train_control,
  weights    = model_weights,
  metric     = "ROC",
  tuneLength = 10
)

cat("Classification Tree training complete.\n\n")

# Predictions on test set
pred_tree      <- predict(model_tree, newdata = test_data)
pred_tree_prob <- predict(model_tree, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")

# Confusion matrix
cm_tree <- confusionMatrix(
  data      = pred_tree,
  reference = test_data$DEFAULT,
  positive  = "Default"
)

# AUC
roc_tree <- roc(
  response  = test_data$DEFAULT,
  predictor = pred_tree_prob[, "Default"],
  levels    = c("No_Default", "Default")
)

# Print all results
cat("=== CLASSIFICATION TREE RESULTS ===\n\n")
cat("Confusion Matrix:\n")
print(cm_tree$table)

cat("\nKey Metrics:\n")
cat("Accuracy: ", round(cm_tree$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("Precision:", round(cm_tree$byClass["Precision"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("Recall:   ", round(cm_tree$byClass["Recall"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("F1 Score: ", round(cm_tree$byClass["F1"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("AUC:      ", round(auc(roc_tree), 3), "\n")
```
```{r tree-visualisation}

# ── Visualising the Decision Tree ────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# This is one of the most powerful features of a classification tree —
# we can actually see the decisions it makes and trace the path for
# any customer.
#
# Each node shows:
# - The splitting condition (e.g. PAY_DELAY_COUNT >= 2)
# - The probability of Default in that branch
# - The percentage of customers reaching that node
#
# This directly connects to our Invisible Debt Trap Flag logic —
# the tree independently discovers that payment delays and repayment
# behaviour are the most important splitting features.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

rpart.plot(
  model_tree$finalModel,
  type     = 4,
  extra    = 104,
  box.palette = c("#27AE60", "#F39C12", "#E67E22", "#C0392B"),
  shadow.col  = "grey80",
  nn          = TRUE,
  fallen.leaves = TRUE,
  main        = "Classification Tree — Default Prediction\nUCI Credit Card Dataset"
)
```

```{r random-forest}

# ── Model 3: Random Forest ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# A random forest builds many decision trees — each trained on a random
# sample of the data and a random subset of features — then combines
# their predictions by majority vote.
#
# This fixes the main weakness of a single tree:
# - A single tree tends to overfit — it memorises the training data
#   rather than learning the general pattern
# - By averaging hundreds of trees built on different samples,
#   the random forest cancels out individual errors
#
# This is the ensemble method covered in Week 8 of FIT5145.
# We expect it to outperform both logistic regression and the single tree.
#
# Note: Random Forest takes longer to train — typically 3 to 5 minutes.
# This is normal. Do not close RStudio while it runs.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Training Random Forest — this will take 3 to 5 minutes...\n\n")

set.seed(42)

model_rf <- train(
  DEFAULT ~ .,
  data      = train_data,
  method    = "rf",
  trControl = train_control,
  weights   = model_weights,
  metric    = "ROC",
  tuneLength = 3,
  ntree      = 200
)

cat("Random Forest training complete.\n\n")

# Predictions on test set
pred_rf      <- predict(model_rf, newdata = test_data)
pred_rf_prob <- predict(model_rf, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")

# Confusion matrix
cm_rf <- confusionMatrix(
  data      = pred_rf,
  reference = test_data$DEFAULT,
  positive  = "Default"
)

# AUC
roc_rf <- roc(
  response  = test_data$DEFAULT,
  predictor = pred_rf_prob[, "Default"],
  levels    = c("No_Default", "Default")
)

# Print all results
cat("=== RANDOM FOREST RESULTS ===\n\n")
cat("Confusion Matrix:\n")
print(cm_rf$table)

cat("\nKey Metrics:\n")
cat("Accuracy: ", round(cm_rf$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("Precision:", round(cm_rf$byClass["Precision"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("Recall:   ", round(cm_rf$byClass["Recall"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("F1 Score: ", round(cm_rf$byClass["F1"] * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("AUC:      ", round(auc(roc_rf), 3), "\n")
```

```{r model-comparison-note}

# ──Explanation on  Recall Matters Most For This Project ─────────────────────────────────
#
# For a consumer debt stress early warning system, missing a genuinely
# at-risk customer (False Negative) is more harmful than incorrectly
# flagging a safe customer (False Positive).
#
# A False Negative means a customer in real debt stress receives no warning
# and continues without intervention until the situation worsens.
# A False Positive means a safe customer receives an unnecessary alert
# — they can simply dismiss it.
#
# This asymmetry of costs means Recall should be our primary evaluation
# metric, not accuracy. By this measure, the Classification Tree performs
# best at 63% recall, followed by Logistic Regression at 60%.
#
# Random Forest achieves higher accuracy (81.6%) but only catches 38%
# of actual defaulters — making it the least suitable model for our purpose
# despite appearing strongest on the accuracy metric.
#
# This finding will be discussed in the report's Demonstration section.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Model comparison — Recall focused:\n\n")
cat("Classification Tree: 63.0% recall — recommended for this project\n")
cat("Logistic Regression: 60.0% recall — strong interpretable baseline\n")
cat("Random Forest:       38.0% recall — highest accuracy but misses\n")
cat("                                     most actual defaulters\n\n")
cat("For a debt stress early warning system, recall is the priority metric.\n")
cat("Missing a real case is worse than a false alarm.\n")
```

```{r load-rba-c1}

# ── Loading RBA C1 Credit Card Data-- ──────────────────────────────────────────
#
# The RBA file has 11 header rows before the actual data begins.
# We skip those and load from row 12 onwards.
#
# Step 1: Read column names from row 2 separately
# Step 2: Read data starting from row 12
# Step 3: Assign column names and convert dates
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Step 1 — Get column names from row 2 of the file
rba_headers <- read_excel(
  "dataset/c01hist(RBA_1).xlsx",
  skip      = 1,
  n_max     = 1,
  col_names = FALSE
)

col_names_vec <- as.character(rba_headers[1, ])
cat("Number of columns found:", length(col_names_vec), "\n\n")


# Step 2 — Load the actual data starting at row 12
rba_raw <- read_excel(
  "dataset/c01hist(RBA_1).xlsx",
  skip      = 11,
  col_names = FALSE
)

cat("Rows loaded:", nrow(rba_raw), "\n")
cat("Columns loaded:", ncol(rba_raw), "\n\n")


# Step 3 — Assign column names
# The number of header columns and data columns must match
# If they differ we use the data column count
if (length(col_names_vec) == ncol(rba_raw)) {
  names(rba_raw) <- col_names_vec
} else {
  names(rba_raw)[1] <- "Date"
  cat("Note: column count mismatch — date column named manually\n")
}


# Step 4 — Show all column names so we can find the ones we need
cat("All column names in RBA C1 file:\n")
for (i in seq_along(names(rba_raw))) {
  cat(i, ":", names(rba_raw)[i], "\n")
}
```

```{r process-rba-c1}
  

# ── Step 1: Select Relevant Columns

# ──────────────────────────────────────────

# ----Complete Data Cleaning--------------- 

rba_selected <- rba_raw %>%
  select(
    Date_Raw          = `Title`,
    Balances_Interest = `Balances accruing interest`,
    Total_Balances    = `Total balances`,
    Repayments        = `Repayments`,
    Personal_Balances = `Total balances: personal cards`
  )

cat("Columns selected:", ncol(rba_selected), "\n")
cat("Rows before cleaning:", nrow(rba_selected), "\n\n")


# ── Step 2: Standardise Column Names ─────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Original column names have spaces, mixed case, and colons.
# We standardise to lowercase with underscores — consistent with
# the UCI dataset column naming convention we used earlier.

rba_selected <- rba_selected %>%
  rename_with(~ tolower(gsub(" ", "_", gsub(":", "", .x))))

cat("Standardised column names:\n")
print(names(rba_selected))
cat("\n")


# ── Step 3: Convert Date Column-- ───────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# The date column contains Excel serial numbers.
# Excel dates start from 1899-12-30 due to a known Excel quirk.
# We convert to proper R Date objects.

rows_before_date_filter <- nrow(rba_selected)

rba_selected <- rba_selected %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(as.numeric(date_raw), origin = "1899-12-30")
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(date)) %>%
  select(-date_raw)

rows_removed_date <- rows_before_date_filter - nrow(rba_selected)
cat("Rows removed due to invalid dates:", rows_removed_date, "\n")
cat("Date range after conversion:", format(min(rba_selected$date)),
    "to", format(max(rba_selected$date)), "\n\n")


# ── Step 4: Convert Balance Columns to Numeric ───────────────────────────────

rba_selected <- rba_selected %>%
  mutate(
    balances_interest = as.numeric(balances_interest),
    total_balances    = as.numeric(total_balances),
    repayments        = as.numeric(repayments),
    personal_balances = as.numeric(personal_balances)
  )


# ── Step 5: Missing Value Audit-- ───────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Explicitly count missing values in each column before removing them.

cat("Missing value audit:\n")
missing_check <- colSums(is.na(rba_selected))
print(missing_check)
cat("\n")

rows_before_na <- nrow(rba_selected)

rba_selected <- rba_selected %>%
  filter(!is.na(balances_interest), !is.na(total_balances))

rows_removed_na <- rows_before_na - nrow(rba_selected)
cat("Rows removed due to missing balance values:", rows_removed_na, "\n\n")


# ── Step 6: Check for Negative Values ────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Credit card balances and repayments should never be negative.
# A negative balance would mean the bank owes the customer money at
# aggregate level — impossible in Australian credit card market data.

cat("Negative value check:\n")
cat("Negative balances_interest:", sum(rba_selected$balances_interest < 0,
                                       na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
cat("Negative total_balances:   ", sum(rba_selected$total_balances < 0,
                                       na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
cat("Negative repayments:       ", sum(rba_selected$repayments < 0,
                                       na.rm = TRUE), "\n\n")


# ── Step 7: Check for Zero Values ────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# A total balance of exactly zero for an entire month is suspicious —
# it would mean no Australian held a credit card balance that month.

cat("Zero value check:\n")
cat("Months with zero total_balances:", sum(rba_selected$total_balances == 0,
                                             na.rm = TRUE), "\n\n")


# ── Step 8: Check for Duplicate Dates--- #────────────────────────────────────────

dup_dates <- sum(duplicated(rba_selected$date))
cat("Duplicate dates found:", dup_dates, "\n\n")


# ── Step 9: Check for Impossible Revolving Ratios
# ────────────────────────────
# Balances accruing interest cannot exceed total balances.
# A ratio above 100% or below 0% indicates a data error.

rba_selected <- rba_selected %>%
  mutate(
    revolving_ratio = round(balances_interest / total_balances * 100, 1)
  )

cat("Revolving ratio range check:\n")
cat("Minimum ratio:", min(rba_selected$revolving_ratio, na.rm = TRUE), "%\n")
cat("Maximum ratio:", max(rba_selected$revolving_ratio, na.rm = TRUE), "%\n")
cat("Rows above 100%:", sum(rba_selected$revolving_ratio > 100,
                             na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
cat("Rows below 0%:  ", sum(rba_selected$revolving_ratio < 0,
                             na.rm = TRUE), "\n\n")


# ── Step 10: Check Time Series Continuity ────────────────────────────────────
#
# Monthly data should have no gaps. If dates jump by more than
# one month, there is a gap in the time series.

date_diffs <- as.numeric(diff(rba_selected$date))
gaps <- sum(date_diffs > 35)
cat("Gaps in monthly time series (jumps > 35 days):", gaps, "\n\n")


# ── Step 11: Filter to 2015 Onwards #──────────────────────────────────────────

rba_clean <- rba_selected %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("2015-01-01")) %>%
  arrange(date)

cat("─────────────────────────────────────────────\n")
cat("RBA C1 clean dataset ready.\n")
cat("Date range:", format(min(rba_clean$date)), "to",
    format(max(rba_clean$date)), "\n")
cat("Total months:", nrow(rba_clean), "\n")
cat("Missing values remaining:", sum(is.na(rba_clean)), "\n")
cat("─────────────────────────────────────────────\n")

```


```{r fix-rba-dates}

# ── Diagnosing the Date Column ────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# First we check what class read_excel actually gave us for the date column.
# If it is already a Date or POSIXct, we should not apply numeric conversion.
# If it is numeric, we apply the Excel origin conversion.
# If it is character, we need a different approach.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Class of date_raw column:", class(rba_raw[[1]]), "\n")
cat("First 5 values in date column:\n")
print(head(rba_raw[[1]], 5))
cat("\n")

# Fix: convert based on actual class
rba_selected <- rba_raw %>%
  select(
    date_raw          = 1,
    balances_interest = `Balances accruing interest`,
    total_balances    = `Total balances`,
    repayments        = `Repayments`,
    personal_balances = `Total balances: personal cards`
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Handle all three possible cases for the date column
    date = case_when(
      # Already a Date or POSIXct — just convert directly
      inherits(date_raw, "POSIXct") | inherits(date_raw, "Date") ~
        as.Date(date_raw),
      # Numeric — Excel serial number conversion
      is.numeric(date_raw) ~
        as.Date(as.numeric(date_raw), origin = "1899-12-30"),
      # Character — try parsing as date string
      TRUE ~
        as.Date(as.character(date_raw))
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(date)) %>%
  select(-date_raw)

cat("Date conversion result:\n")
cat("First 5 dates:\n")
print(head(rba_selected$date, 5))
cat("\nLast 5 dates:\n")
print(tail(rba_selected$date, 5))
cat("\nDate range:", format(min(rba_selected$date)),
    "to", format(max(rba_selected$date)), "\n")
```

```{r rba-clean-complete}

# ── Complete the RBA Data Cleaning- ───────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Now that dates are correct we finish cleaning:
# - Convert balance columns to numeric
# - Run the full missing value audit
# - Check for negative and impossible values
# - Check for duplicate dates
# - Filter to 2015 onwards for our analysis window
# - Derive the revolving ratio
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Convert all balance columns to numeric
rba_selected <- rba_selected %>%
  mutate(
    balances_interest = as.numeric(balances_interest),
    total_balances    = as.numeric(total_balances),
    repayments        = as.numeric(repayments),
    personal_balances = as.numeric(personal_balances)
  )


# ── Missing value audit ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Missing value audit before filtering:\n")
print(colSums(is.na(rba_selected)))
cat("\n")

rows_before_na <- nrow(rba_selected)

rba_selected <- rba_selected %>%
  filter(!is.na(balances_interest), !is.na(total_balances))

rows_removed <- rows_before_na - nrow(rba_selected)
cat("Rows removed due to missing balance values:", rows_removed, "\n")
cat("Rows remaining:", nrow(rba_selected), "\n\n")


# ── Negative value check ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("Negative value check:\n")
cat("Negative balances_interest:", sum(rba_selected$balances_interest < 0), "\n")
cat("Negative total_balances:   ", sum(rba_selected$total_balances < 0),    "\n")
cat("Negative repayments:       ", sum(rba_selected$repayments < 0, na.rm = TRUE), "\n\n")


# ── Duplicate date check ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

dup_dates <- sum(duplicated(rba_selected$date))
cat("Duplicate dates found:", dup_dates, "\n\n")


# ── Derive revolving ratio ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Revolving ratio = balances accruing interest / total balances
# This is our key Australian context metric.
# It shows what share of all Australian credit card debt is currently
# rolling over with interest — the core indicator of debt trap behaviour.

rba_selected <- rba_selected %>%
  mutate(
    revolving_ratio = round(balances_interest / total_balances * 100, 1)
  )

cat("Revolving ratio range check:\n")
cat("Minimum:", min(rba_selected$revolving_ratio), "%\n")
cat("Maximum:", max(rba_selected$revolving_ratio), "%\n")
cat("Any above 100%:", sum(rba_selected$revolving_ratio > 100), "\n")
cat("Any below 0%:  ", sum(rba_selected$revolving_ratio < 0),   "\n\n")


# ── Filter to 2015 onwards ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

rba_clean <- rba_selected %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("2015-01-01")) %>%
  arrange(date)


# ── Final summary ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

cat("─────────────────────────────────────────────\n")
cat("RBA C1 clean dataset ready.\n\n")
cat("Date range:", format(min(rba_clean$date)),
    "to", format(max(rba_clean$date)), "\n")
cat("Total months:", nrow(rba_clean), "\n")
cat("Missing values remaining:", sum(is.na(rba_clean)), "\n\n")

cat("Revolving ratio — key findings:\n")
cat("Latest value:  ",
    rba_clean$revolving_ratio[nrow(rba_clean)], "%  on",
    format(max(rba_clean$date)), "\n")
cat("Highest since 2015:",
    max(rba_clean$revolving_ratio), "% on",
    format(rba_clean$date[which.max(rba_clean$revolving_ratio)]), "\n")
cat("Lowest since 2015: ",
    min(rba_clean$revolving_ratio), "% on",
    format(rba_clean$date[which.min(rba_clean$revolving_ratio)]), "\n")
cat("─────────────────────────────────────────────\n")
```


```{r rba-events-chart}

# ── Australian Revolving Ratio With Economic Event Annotations ────────────────
#
# This chart tells the story of WHY the revolving ratio moved the way it did.

# and credit card repayment behaviour.
#
# 1. COVID-19 (Mar 2020): Government stimulus gave households extra cash.
#    Many used it to pay down credit card debt. Revolving ratio fell.
#
# 2. Ukraine War / Global Inflation (Feb 2022): Energy and food prices
#    spiked globally. Australians used credit cards for daily expenses.
#
# 3. RBA Rate Hikes Begin (May 2022): RBA raised cash rate 13 times from
#    0.1% to 4.35% — fastest rate-rise cycle in Australian history.
#
# 4. Red Sea Crisis (Dec 2023): Iran-backed Houthi forces attacked Red Sea
#    shipping lanes. Shipping costs spiked 300%. Australian import prices
#    rose, adding further cost-of-living pressure on households.
#
# 5. RBA Rate Cuts Begin (Feb 2025): RBA began cutting rates.
#    Some mortgage relief but credit card stress remains elevated.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

rba_plot <- rba_clean %>%
  mutate(total_balances_bn = total_balances / 1000)

events <- data.frame(
  date   = as.Date(c("2020-03-01", "2022-02-24",
                      "2022-05-01", "2023-12-01", "2025-02-01")),

              "Ukraine War\nGlobal Inflation",

  colour = c("#2471A3", "#8E44AD", "#E74C3C", "#D35400", "#27AE60")
)

latest_point <- rba_plot %>% slice_tail(n = 1)

covid_low <- rba_plot %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("2021-01-01"),

  filter(revolving_ratio == min(revolving_ratio))

p <- ggplot(rba_plot, aes(x = date)) +

  annotate("rect",

           fill  = "#E74C3C") +

  annotate("rect",
           xmin  = as.Date("2025-02-01"),

           ymax  = Inf,

  geom_line(aes(y = revolving_ratio),
            colour    = "#2C3E50",

  geom_smooth(aes(y = revolving_ratio),
              method    = "loess",
              span      = 0.25,
              colour    = "#E74C3C",
              se        = FALSE,
              linewidth = 1.4) +

  geom_vline(data      = events,
             aes(xintercept = date,
                 colour     = colour),
             linetype  = "dashed",

             alpha     = 0.8) +

  geom_label(data = events,
             aes(x      = date,
                 y      = y_pos,
                 label  = label,
                 colour = colour),
             fill          = "white",
             size          = 2.8,
             fontface      = "bold",
             label.padding = unit(0.2, "lines"),
             label.size    = 0.3) +

  geom_point(data   = latest_point,
             aes(y  = revolving_ratio),
             colour = "#C0392B",
             size   = 4) +

  geom_label(data      = latest_point,
             aes(y     = revolving_ratio,

             nudge_x   = -200,

  scale_x_date(date_breaks  = "1 year",

  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(44, 68),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"),
                     breaks = seq(44, 68, by = 4)) +

  labs(
    title    = "Australian Credit Card Revolving Ratio: 2015–2026",
    subtitle = "Share of total balances accruing interest monthly  |  Red shading = RBA rate hike cycle  |  Green shading = rate cut period",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Revolving Ratio (%)",
    caption  = "Source: RBA Statistical Table C1 (rba.gov.au)  |  Revolving ratio = Balances accruing interest / Total balances  |  Analysis by Shah Md Anasullah"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 9),
    plot.caption       = element_text(colour = "grey50", size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )

print(p)
```

```{r probability-flag-mapping}

# ── Mapping Model Probabilities to Flag Categories ────────────────────────────
#
# The ML model predicts a probability of default for each customer.
# The Invisible Debt Trap Flag is the business-facing output. It converts
# the predicted probability into a simple risk category that a user can
# understand: Stable, Watch, Early Flag, or High Risk.
#
# For this demonstration, we use the Classification Tree because it achieved
# the strongest recall among the tested models. Recall is important here
# because the project is designed as an early warning system, where missing
# a genuinely risky customer is more harmful than flagging too cautiously.
#
# The probability bands are estimated from the training prediction distribution
# and then applied to the test set. This avoids designing the flag thresholds
# directly from the test data.
#
# These bands are demonstration thresholds only. A real Australian system
# would need calibration using local customer-consented data from statements
# or CDR/open banking.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


# Step 1 — Get predicted probabilities from the Classification Tree
# We already have pred_tree_prob from model training
# Column "Default" contains the probability of default for each customer

default_probs_test <- pred_tree_prob[, "Default"]

cat("Predicted probability summary on test set:\n")
print(summary(default_probs_test))
cat("\n")


# Step 2 — Get training predictions to set probability band thresholds
# We use the saved cross-validation predictions from the training phase
# This ensures our bands are defined from training data, not test data

train_cv_probs <- model_tree$pred %>%
  filter(cp == model_tree$bestTune$cp) %>%
  pull(Default)

# If CV predictions are not available, use training set predictions directly
if (length(train_cv_probs) == 0) {
  train_cv_probs <- predict(model_tree,
                             newdata = train_data,
                             type    = "prob")[, "Default"]
}

cat("Training probability distribution (used to set band thresholds):\n")
print(quantile(train_cv_probs,
               probs = c(0.25, 0.40, 0.60, 0.75, 0.90)))
cat("\n")


# Step 3 — Define probability bands from training distribution
# We use natural breaks in the training probability distribution
# rather than arbitrary fixed values

threshold_watch      <- round(quantile(train_cv_probs, 0.40), 3)
threshold_early_flag <- round(quantile(train_cv_probs, 0.65), 3)
threshold_high_risk  <- round(quantile(train_cv_probs, 0.82), 3)

cat("Probability band thresholds (from training distribution):\n")
cat("Stable:     probability < ", threshold_watch, "\n")
cat("Watch:      probability ", threshold_watch,
    "to <", threshold_early_flag, "\n")
cat("Early Flag: probability ", threshold_early_flag,
    "to <", threshold_high_risk, "\n")
cat("High Risk:  probability >=", threshold_high_risk, "\n\n")


# Step 4 — Apply thresholds to test set probabilities
test_flag_mapped <- data.frame(
  Actual_Default = test_data$DEFAULT,
  Default_Prob   = default_probs_test
) %>%
  mutate(
    ML_Flag = case_when(
      Default_Prob >= threshold_high_risk  ~ "High Risk",
      Default_Prob >= threshold_early_flag ~ "Early Flag",
      Default_Prob >= threshold_watch      ~ "Watch",
      TRUE                                 ~ "Stable"
    ),
    ML_Flag = factor(ML_Flag,
                     levels  = c("Stable", "Watch",
                                 "Early Flag", "High Risk"),
                     ordered = TRUE)
  )


# Step 5 — Check flag distribution and default rates per flag
cat("=== ML PROBABILITY FLAG DISTRIBUTION ===\n\n")

flag_summary <- test_flag_mapped %>%
  group_by(ML_Flag) %>%
  summarise(
    Customers    = n(),
    Pct          = round(n() / nrow(test_flag_mapped) * 100, 1),
    Avg_Prob     = round(mean(Default_Prob) * 100, 1),
    Default_Rate = round(mean(Actual_Default == "Default") * 100, 1)
  )

print(flag_summary)
cat("\n")
cat("Note: Default rate should increase from Stable to High Risk.\n")
cat("This validates that probability bands are meaningful.\n")
```

```{r probability-mapping-chart}

# ── Visualising the Probability-to-Flag Mapping ───────────────────────────────
#
# Two charts side by side:
# Left: distribution of predicted probabilities coloured by flag category
# Right: default rate per flag category with customer counts
#
# Together they show both HOW the probabilities are distributed AND
# whether the flag categories are genuinely separating risk levels.
#
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

flag_colours <- c("Stable"     = "#27AE60",
                  "Watch"      = "#F39C12",
                  "Early Flag" = "#E67E22",
                  "High Risk"  = "#C0392B")

# ── Left chart — probability distribution by flag ────────────────────────────

p_left <- ggplot(test_flag_mapped,
                 aes(x = Default_Prob, fill = ML_Flag)) +

  geom_histogram(bins     = 40,
                 colour   = "white",

             linetype   = "dashed",

  geom_vline(xintercept = threshold_early_flag,

             linetype   = "dashed",

  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(round(x * 100), "%"),
    limits = c(0.2, 0.95)
  ) +

  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +

  labs(
    title    = "Predicted Default Probability Distribution",
    subtitle = "Colour shows assigned flag category",
    x        = "Predicted Probability of Default",
    y        = "Number of Customers",
    fill     = NULL
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position  = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )


# ── Right chart — default rate by flag with counts ───────────────────────────

p_right <- flag_summary %>%

  geom_bar(stat   = "identity",

            fontface = "bold") +

  scale_fill_manual(values = flag_colours) +

  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 75),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +

  labs(
    title    = "Default Rate by Flag Category",
    subtitle = "Validates probability bands are meaningful",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Actual Default Rate (%)",
    fill     = NULL
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position    = "none",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()
  )


# ── Combine both charts ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────

grid.arrange(
  p_left, p_right,
  ncol = 2,
  top  = grid::textGrob(
    "Invisible Debt Trap Flag — Probability Mapping Validation",
    gp = grid::gpar(fontface = "bold", fontsize = 13)
  )
)
```
